#smile

Contents
Tens of thousands 
united for a smile
We launched with love for our country and our people.

Driven by this passion, we have grown steadily, earning 
trust and appreciation around the world.

In 2025, as 
the national flag carrier, we continued to elevate our 
performance with the same passion and dedication.

What makes us strong is not only our next-generation 
aircraft, advanced technology, or expanding flight 
network, but also the tens of thousands of employees 
who work with passion and treat every guest with the 
same care.

From cockpit to technical teams, from cabin crews to 
operations centers, and from ground services to digital 
teams, our entire family will work with the same purpose 
and passion to make our guests happy in 2026.

#happyguests
Throughout 2025, our passengers were at 
the heart of every action we took. A 10-point 
increase in our Net Promoter Score and 
soaring satisfaction rates were compelling 
indicators that our efforts resonated and 
brought smiles to faces. From catering to 
digital services and from baggage tracking 
innovations to our flight network expansion, 
every touchpoint is designed with one goal 
in mind: our guests’ happiness. At Turkish 
Airlines, every journey begins with care, and 
every flight leads to satisfaction.
85.6%
Customer Satisfaction Rate

#moretocome
As we left behind a year filled with challenges, we once 
again drew strength from the smiles of our guests. From 
cabin crews to technical teams, from digital units to 
field staff, we worked as one united team to deliver the 
highest level of service to our passengers. Thanks to our 
collective efforts, we were named Best Airline in Europe 
by Skytrax, winning eight awards. We consistently strive 
every day to provide safer, more punctual, and more 
comfortable flights, working tirelessly to further 
enhance customer satisfaction.

#ourwordisourbond
In 2025, we extended our exemplary service approach 
into an even stronger commitment: to be an airline 
that places customer focus at the heart of its decisions, 
keeps its promises, inspires trust, and stands by its 
passengers. Hospitality training for cabin crew and 
ground staff and live travel notifications via our mobile 
app were key steps in this journey, as were enhanced 
self-service capabilities across digital channels, 
improved on-time departure performance, and the 
expansion of inflight internet across the fleet. 
A truly satisfying flight is one where every promise 
is fulfilled. Accordingly, we implemented these 
developments to ensure that “customer focus” is 
a tangible experience rather than a mere promise. 
Standing by our commitment— “With trust and care, 
we transform every journey into an experience beyond 
expectations”—we will continue to deliver a superior 
experience at every touchpoint.
80.6%
TK on-time 
departure rate

#collaboration
In 2025, we strengthened global connectivity through a 
joint venture with Thai Airways, a new partnership with Air 
Transat in Canada, and two new codeshare agreements 
in South Africa. Each collaboration was established to 
provide our passengers with additional options, faster 
connections, and a more seamless travel experience. 
More than a growth strategy, this global network 
signals a system where customer satisfaction is 
transformed into flight routes.
Turkish Airlines is no longer just growing; it is building 
a customer satisfaction ecosystem together with 
all its stakeholders. Each new partnership pushes the 
boundaries of our success even further.
* The number of actively flown countries is 124.
** A total of 530 destinations are served through partnerships.
IN 132 COUNTRIES*
356 DESTINATIONS**

#valueloaded
For Turkish Airlines, cargo transportation represents not 
only the movement of goods, but also a responsibility 
that connects countries, economies, and lives. 
Leveraging the power of one of the world’s most extensive 
flight networks, Turkish Cargo continued to be a reliable 
pillar of global trade in 2025.
We continue to deepen our capabilities through 
international cargo partnerships. New expansions and 
growing logistics collaborations across the globe have 
marked important milestones in our long-term growth 
vision for cargo operations. Behind every shipment lies a 
dedicated effort—teams racing against time and tens of 
thousands of employees who carry out their work with 
passion. For us, cargo is not just a load being transported; 
it is a promise delivered with trust.

#ourcarbonneutraljourney
In line with our 2050 carbon-neutral target, we 
carry out initiatives to reduce carbon emissions 
by deploying more fuel-efficient aircraft, emission 
reduction programs, and digital applications 
that support operational efficiency. In our flight 
operations, we prioritize reducing fuel consumption 
and optimizing the usage of resources. We 
complement these actions with our technical 
evaluations in the field of Sustainable Aviation Fuel 
(SAF).
Our fleet investments and operational 
improvements supporting our transition toward 
lower carbon emissions are managed within a 
holistic framework, together with sustainable 
financing instruments. In this context, as we 
progress toward our carbon-neutral target, 
we adopt a measurable and transparent 
emission management approach.

Carbon emissions 
avoided in 2025

factor of 3.16 tons of CO₂ per ton of fossil jet fuel.

14 / INTRODUCTION
This is the first integrated annual 
report of Türk Hava Yolları Anonim 
Ortaklığı (“Turkish Airlines,” or “the 
Company”).

It presents our strategy, 
business model, governance, risk 
and opportunity framework, and 
our financial and non-financial 
performance as an integrated 
whole.

Our goal is to convey our 
value creation capacity not only 
through results, but also through the 
processes by which we achieve these 
results and how we transform our 
resources.

Our report covers the period from 
January 1, 2025, to December 31, 
2025.

Where necessary to accurately 
interpret trends, we also include 
actual results from 2021 to 2024.

We address our short- (one year), 
medium- (one to five years), and long-
term (more than five years) targets 
together within this framework.

Unless otherwise stated, the data 
shared in the report refers to the 
consolidated structure, including our 
subsidiaries and affiliates.

Our Value Creation Model is central 
to our integrated reporting approach.

We assess how we use the six 
capitals—financial, manufactured, 
intellectual, human, social and 
relationship, and natural capital—
within our business model, how 
we transform them through our 
activities, and their impacts on 
our stakeholders.

We assess how we use the six 
capitals—financial, manufactured, 
intellectual, human, social and 
relationship, and natural capital—
within our business model, how 
we transform them through our 
activities, and their impacts on 
our stakeholders.

This allows us to 
present the link between financial 
performance and environmental, 
social, and governance indicators in 
a clearer, more traceable, and more 
integrated way for decision-making 
processes.

We use a double materiality 
approach to develop the content 
of the report.

On one hand, we 
assess the environmental and social 
impacts of our operations;

on the 
other, we analyze the impact of 
sustainability risks and opportunities 
on our financial results, operational 
continuity, and strategic direction.

Within this framework, we ensure 
compliance with international 
frameworks, including the Türkiye 
Sustainability Reporting Standards 
(TSRS), the <IR> Integrated Reporting 
Framework, IFRS S1 and IFRS S2, 
GRI, TCFD, and SASB.

Our goal is not 
only to ensure compliance, but also 
to establish a stakeholder-focused, 
comparable, and reliable information 
structure.

We report our financial data in line 
with our audited consolidated 
financial statements.

We continue 
to strengthen data quality, 
measurement methods, and internal 
control processes for non-financial 
indicators.

We have designed this integrated 
annual report to be read in 
conjunction with our financial 
reports, TSRS-compliant disclosures, 
and Public Disclosure Platform (KAP) 
announcements.

In this way, we 
strengthen the connection between 
our various reporting documents and 
present our value creation story to 
stakeholders as a cohesive whole.

Selected indicators in this report 
have undergone a limited external 
audit by PwC Türkiye in accordance 
with the “ISAE 3000” and “ISAE 3410” 
standards.

The list of indicators and 
the scope of the assurance audit 
can be found on pages 505–507 
of the report.

The greenhouse gas 
statements for 2025 disclosed in 
the report have been verified by 
an independent organization in 
accordance with the requirements 
of the TS EN ISO 14064-3:2019.

Esteemed Shareholders, Customers, 
Business Partners, and Employees,
As Turkish Airlines, while expanding our 
scale in 2025, we focused on further 
strengthening the foundations that will 
carry us into the future.

As of year-end, 
with a fleet of 516 aircraft, we flew 
to 356 destinations in 132 countries, 
served 92.6 million passengers, and 
increased our consolidated revenues 
to over USD 24.1 billion.

Together 
with more than 100 thousand, 
employees across our parent company 
and subsidiaries, we continued to 
transform this scale into tangible 
value for our country.

By updating 
our 2033 goals with a more forward-
looking perspective, we framed our 
2036 vision.

In addition to growth, we 
have prioritized building a corporate 
structure that is more agile, more 
resilient, and more responsible.

Managing opportunities and 
risks in a growing industry
The year 2025 marked a turning point 
as global aviation entered a period of 
structurally high demand.

According to 
IATA data, industry revenues exceeded 
USD 1 trillion for the first time, 
highlighting aviation’s role as a core 
infrastructure for global trade, tourism, 
Strong operations, sustainable 
growth
Sustaining this scale requires well-
balanced capacity and network 
management.

In 2025, we maintained 
this balance and expanded our 
operational capacity in line with 
demand.

Our Available Seat Kilometers 
(ASK) rose 7.5% year-on-year to 273.2 
billion.

Our overall passenger load 
factor stood at 83.2%, with 82.9% 
on international routes and 86.0% 
on domestic routes.

Our overall passenger load

on international routes and 86.0% 
on domestic routes.

The number of 
international-to-international transfer 
passengers rose by 12.8%, reaching 
35.7 million.

Our total cargo and mail 
volume climbed by 8.4% to 2.2 million 
tons.

In 2025, we expanded our flight 
network in a balanced yet determined 
manner.

With the launch of four new 
international routes, we also resumed 
services to five destinations.

In line with 
our projected average annual growth 
rate of approximately 7% through 2036, 
we deepened our presence on routes 
where demand is growing—particularly 
in the Asia-Pacific and North America 
regions, as well as in high-potential 
Latin American markets.

We maintained 
our status as the airline flying to the 
most countries in the world, operating 
across 356 destinations in 132 countries 
across six continents.

Preparing our fleet and 
infrastructure for the future
We currently lead a transformation that 
will double our current scale over the 
next decade.

Our fleet, which reached 
516 aircraft by the end of 2025, reflects 
clear progress toward our 1,000-aircraft 
fleet plan extending into the next ten 
years.

With an average fleet age of 9.9 
years, we maintain a distinct advantage 
in fuel efficiency, safety, maintenance 
costs, and passenger comfort.

Marking 
a milestone in this journey was the 
"TK Aile - TK Family (TK being the IATA 
airline designator for Turkish Airlines)" 
aircraft.

As the 500th aircraft to join our 
fleet, its livery featured the photos of 
our 100 thousand employees, signifying 
the beginning of our next phase, i.e.

the 
second 500.

and cultural interaction.

While supply 
chain challenges, delays in aircraft and 
engine production, and geopolitical 
developments continued to pressure 
the sector, we maintained our balanced 
growth through geographical 
diversification, a strong balance sheet, 
flexible capacity planning, and effective 
risk management.

The Turkish economy continued its 
nearly quarter-century journey of 
uninterrupted growth, achieving new 
records in 2025.

The Turkish economy continued its 
nearly quarter-century journey of 
uninterrupted growth, achieving new 
records in 2025.

With USD 273.4 billion 
in goods exports and USD 122.6 billion 
in services exports, total exports 
reached USD 396 billion.

The size of the 
economy exceeded USD 1.56 trillion, 
marking a historic level and further 
consolidating Türkiye’s position in 
the global economy.

By boosting our 
exports from USD 18.2 billion in 2024 to 
USD 19.3 billion in 2025—6% growth—
we once again became Türkiye’s leading 
exporter, contributing USD 9 billion 
in net foreign currency inflow to the 
national economy.

We define our role 
within the Century of Türkiye vision 
as a strategic actor connecting our 
country’s production, employment, 
exports, and technological capabilities 
to the world.

In line with our 2033 and 2036 targets, 
we continue to renew our fleet within 
a long-term strategic framework.

The 
backbone of this plan was established 
through our Airbus order agreement 
in 2023.

Following our agreement 
with Boeing, in 2025, we activated a 
new order package in the long-haul 
segment.

Through our cooperations 
with aircraft and engine manufacturers, 
we are steadily increasing the share of 
next-generation, low-emission aircraft 
in our fleet, optimizing for range, 
capacity, and fuel efficiency.

In 2025, we also completed the 
processes of eight strategic 
investments.

With their foundations 
laid in early 2026, these investments 
have a total value exceeding TRY 
100 billion and are shaping the 
infrastructure that will support this 
fleet architecture.

The key components 
of our vision to establish Turkish 
Airlines as a permanent global aviation 
hub include the wide-body engine 
maintenance center at Istanbul Airport, 
the world’s largest catering facility, 
the second phase of SmartIST, and the 
first phase of the Florya Flight Training 
Center.

Expanding value creation with 
our Group companies
In 2025, together with our parent 
company and subsidiaries, we provided 
employment to approximately 100 
thousand, people.

Expanding value creation with 
our Group companies
In 2025, together with our parent 
company and subsidiaries, we provided 
employment to approximately 100 
thousand, people.

With the year-end 
revenues of our subsidiaries exceeding 
USD 14 billion, our growth contributed 
not only to Türkiye’s employment 
and exports, but also directly to the 
production and R&D capacity of the 
aviation industry.

On the passenger side, SunExpress and 
AJet stand out as two complementary 
business models addressing different 
customer segments.

A low-cost 
model based in Sabiha Gökçen and 
Esenboğa airports, AJet increased 
our accessibility in domestic routes 
and nearby regions, furthering the 
efficient utilization of growing capacity 
at all these airports.

Celebrating its 
35th anniversary in 2025, SunExpress 
continued to expand its flight network 
and carried approximately 16 million 
passengers with a fleet of 85 aircraft.

Having doubled its fleet over the past 
five years by accelerating its growth, 
SunExpress is expected to maintain its 
sustainable growth trajectory in the 
coming period.

Meanwhile, Widect, 
our cargo brand focused on small and 
medium-sized exporters, significantly 
increased its revenues in 2025, adding 
a new Türkiye-based trade channel to 
Turkish Cargo’s global network.

18 / INTRODUCTION

Our “One Team: Passionately Turkish” 
approach, aimed at enhancing the 
customer experience, further matured 
in 2025.

This cultural transformation 
program merges Turkish hospitality 
with contemporary service standards to 
deliver a recognizable, consistent, and 
high-quality Turkish Airlines experience, 
even across all routes and flights.

Extending this approach beyond 
our flights, we conduct promotional 
activities in our strategic markets 
through “Connect to Türkiye” events.

Extending this approach beyond 
our flights, we conduct promotional 
activities in our strategic markets 
through “Connect to Türkiye” events.

Through these events, we showcase 
Türkiye’s rich heritage, natural beauty, 
and deep historical and cultural legacy 
to tourism and travel authorities, 
aviation stakeholders, sales agencies, 
media representatives, opinion leaders, 
and influencers.

By also hosting such 
events within Türkiye, we offer leading 
figures from the tourism and travel 
industry the opportunity to experience 
these values firsthand.

Our experience-oriented approach 
and practices continue to receive 
recognition in international evaluations.

In 2025, we were honored by Skytrax 
with the awards for “Best Airline 
in Europe,” “World’s Best Business 
Class Catering,” and “Best Airline in 
Europe for Design.” Additionally, APEX 
affirmed our consistent performance in 
customer satisfaction, cabin services, 
and operational excellence by awarding 
us the “World Class 2025” title, along 
with “Best Inflight Entertainment in 
Europe” and “Best Wi-Fi in Europe.”
Sustainability lies at the juncture 
of our entire strategy.

Our goal to 
become a carbon-neutral airline by 
2050 is a key reference point in every 
strategic decision we make—from 
fleet planning and fuel sourcing to 
waste management and financing.

We oversee our projects in this area, 
consolidated under the “Tomorrow-On-
Board” framework in 2024, in alignment 
with the United Nations Sustainable 
Development Goals.

In addition to supporting the safety 
and operational continuity of our fleet, 
Turkish Technic continues to expand 
the maintenance, repair, and overhaul 
services provided to international 
airlines.

By 2033, we plan to increase 
our maintenance capacity to 24 
hangars and 102 maintenance slots, 
and to generate a sizeable portion of 
our revenues from foreign carriers.

Furthermore, through the Authorized 
Maintenance Center established at 
Istanbul Airport in collaboration with 
Rolls-Royce, we aim to position Türkiye 
as a global hub for engine maintenance 
and engineering.

Our fully owned subsidiary TCI, 
which consolidates our aircraft cabin 
equipment manufacturing under 
one roof, completed its first certified 
seat project, Milligram, in 2025.

Our fully owned subsidiary TCI, 
which consolidates our aircraft cabin 
equipment manufacturing under 
one roof, completed its first certified 
seat project, Milligram, in 2025.

Combining cabin comfort, weight 
reduction, and efficiency through 
domestic engineering capabilities, this 
seat was first introduced in Boeing 
aircraft for AJet operations, followed 
by deployment across our Airbus 
fleet.

As the national flag carrier, we 
also began offering the domestically 
developed EpiankaPlus seats by TCI 
on our 500th aircraft, the A350-900, 
further enhancing the travel experience 
while reaffirming our commitment to 
representing Turkish engineering on a 
global scale.

Our Flight Training Academy, through 
its training activities conducted 
in Efes, Bodrum, Uşak, Adana, 
Kütahya and Aydın, enabled us 
to meet a considerable portion of 
our pilot demand in 2025 with our 
own graduates.

Turkish Technology 
continued to serve as the driving force 
In this context, we aim to increase the 
share of next-generation aircraft with 
lower fuel consumption and improved 
emission profiles to over 90% by 2033.

In both our new aircraft investments 
and cabin modernization initiatives, 
we prioritize fuel efficiency and weight 
reduction as key criteria.

Since 2022, we have expanded the use 
of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)—
initially implemented on selected 
routes—to a broader network.

Through 
three separate Memorandums of 
Understanding signed with Tüpraş, 
Çalık Renewables, and SOCAR, we took 
a major step toward SAF production 
in Türkiye.

As these projects become 
operational, we plan to reduce 
dependency on external supply chains 
while increasing the share of low-
carbon fuels in our operations.

We actively support the “Zero Waste” 
initiative, which has gained strong 
public recognition across Türkiye, and 
implement systematic practices in our 
offices and aircraft to promote waste 
separation, recycling, and the reduction 
of paper and plastic use.

Within the 
scope of our CO2 Mission project, we 
offset emissions generated during our 
employees’ duty travels and provide 
our passengers with transparent and

Our Tax and Compliance Approach
As a joint-stock company subject to full 
tax liability, we are taxed on the income 
we generate both in Türkiye and abroad.

We contribute comprehensively to the 
public sector through corporate income 
tax, Value Added Tax, stamp duty, income 
tax withheld from employees' wages 
(withholding tax), Recycling Contribution 
Fee (GEKAP), tourism levy, and other 
direct and indirect taxes.

Obligations 
arising from international tax law are also 
fulfilled in a timely manner within the 
framework of the relevant legislation.

We consider tax compliance a 
fundamental element of our corporate 
responsibility.

Our tax strategy is based 
on the principles of full compliance 
with legislation, ethical values, and 
transparency.

Accordingly, we regularly 
review our tax processes, closely monitor 
legislative developments, and make 
use of expert consultancy services 
and advance rulings obtained from 
the Revenue Administration, where 
necessary.

Our accounting records are audited 
by independent audit firms;

our tax 
practices are reviewed within the 
framework of both public audits and 
independent external audits.

Through 
our efforts for our group companies and 
international stations, we aim to maintain 
a high standard of tax compliance in all 
countries where we operate.

The Tax Management Procedure 
published within the Company ensures 
that all transactions are subject to 
systematic review for compliance with 
tax legislation, supported by the opinions 
of sworn-in certified public accountants 
where necessary, and that the results are 
shared with the relevant departments.

We also approach tax management 
from a risk management perspective.

We also approach tax management

approach creates a framework that 
strengthens stakeholder confidence

remaining below 4% indicated the 
industry's limited financial flexibility.

even more pronounced.

Disruptions

production and deliveries, and technical 
issues with certain engine types 
continued to limit capacity growth.

financial pressure on airlines.

Adding Value to Stakeholders
Turkish Airlines aims to establish 
long-term and mutually beneficial 
relationships with a wide range of 
stakeholders, from its customers to 
its employees, from its suppliers to its 
business partners, and from regulatory 
authorities to the communities in 
which it operates.

Conducting its 
activities in line with the principles of 
transparency, fairness, responsibility, 
and accountability, the Company 
positions the balanced and sustainable 
consideration of stakeholder 
expectations as a fundamental priority.

The Company aims to create 
sustainable and balanced value 
for all its stakeholders in line with 
the strategic focus areas defined 
within the framework of its 2033 
vision.

In this context, stakeholder 
expectations are regularly monitored 
and analyzed through corporate 
governance principles and structured 
strategic planning processes, and 
are systematically reflected in the 
Company's short, medium, and long-
term targets.

In line with its vision of adding value 
to its stakeholders, Turkish Airlines 
will continue to develop strategic 
collaborations, increase partnership 
projects, and establish long-term 
relationships based on mutual benefit in 
the global aviation ecosystem.

Sustainability Committee
The strategic center of our

Sustainability Committee, which is 
authorized at the Board of Directors

Established in 2021, the

Senior Vice President of Legal and 
Compliance.

Chief Investment and 
Strategy Officer serves as the Vice 
President of the Committee.

at regular intervals and held 
extraordinary meetings as needed, 
adopting a dynamic working model.

following agenda items during these 
meetings:

Strengthening operational 
sustainability,

Reducing carbon emissions,
• 
Expanding the use of Sustainable 
Aviation Fuel (SAF),
• 
Improving resource efficiency and 
reducing waste in supply chain and 
flight operations, and
• 
Complying with national and 
international climate policies and 
regulations.

transparency standards for climate

Standards (TSRS).

Turkish Cargo Continues to Raise 
the Bar
In 2025, the air cargo and logistics 
sector maintained its growth trend 
despite ongoing political and economic 
uncertainties on a global scale.

The 
restructuring of global trade flows, 
supply chain vulnerabilities, and 
geopolitical risks were the main factors 
directly affecting capacity planning and 
pricing dynamics.1
In the air cargo sector, international 
freight tons-kilometers (FTK) increased 
by 4.2%, while capacity supply grew by 
5.1%.

During this period of concurrent 
growth in demand and capacity, the 
fact that supply slightly outpaced 
demand intensified competition, 
making the delicate management of 
the demand-capacity balance even 
more crucial for success in the industry.

Markets in the Far East, Latin America, 
Africa, and Europe were central to 
the increase in demand, thanks to 
activity on both the production and 
consumption sides.

In this context, despite challenging 
industry conditions, Turkish Cargo 
outperformed the global market's 
overall growth rate, increasing its 
freight ton-kilometers by 10.7%.

Thus, as a result of the steps taken and 
strategic decisions made, the demand-
capacity balance was turned in our favor, 
and growth was successfully managed 
without losing focus on profitability.

Fair Compensation
Turkish Airlines conducts its 
compensation management within 
a fair, transparent, and competitive 
framework.

This approach focuses 
not only on meeting legal obligations 
but also on supporting employee 
engagement, motivation, and long-

The principle of “equal pay for

compensation processes, and wage 
differences based on gender, age, 
ethnicity, or any other discriminatory 
factor are strictly not tolerated.

Male 
and female employees performing 
the same job receive equal base pay, 
and salary increases are applied 
equally to all employees, including 
female employees on maternity leave.

Wage differences are shaped only by 
objective criteria such as the level of 
responsibility required by the position, 
seniority, and experience;

the goal is 
to retain talent that contributes to the 
Company in the long term, also taking 
into account sectoral competitive 
conditions.

Compensation determination processes 
are carried out in line with the employee’s 
knowledge, skills, competency level, 
area of responsibility, and individual 
performance, as well as the Company’s 
long-term goals and Human Resources 
policies.

Thanks to this structure, fair 
compensation becomes not just a right, 
but also a strategic human resources 
management tool.

Fuel Price Risk Management
Fuel expenses constitute the largest 
component of operational costs.

Therefore, fluctuations in jet fuel prices 
have the potential to significantly 
impact cash flow and profitability.

To 
keep this impact at a reasonable and 
manageable level, a Fuel Price Hedging 
Strategy is implemented.

Under this 
strategy:
• 
Hedging transactions are carried out 
for up to 24 months,
• 
A hedge position is taken for a 
maximum of 60% of the following 
month's projected fuel consumption,
• 
Swap- and option-based derivative 
instruments, both with and without 
premiums, are used,
• 
Hedging activities may be 
temporarily suspended during 
periods when market prices rise to 
extreme levels, disrupting forecasts.

For hedging purposes, crude oil 
derivative products, which have a high 
correlation with jet fuel and greater 
market depth, are preferred as the 
underlying asset.

Additionally, the fuel 
surcharge, which is a component of 
ticket prices and is determined based 
on international market conditions and 
the competitive environment, serves as 
a complementary element in managing 
fuel price risk.

When managing fuel price risk, 
the Company closely monitors not 
only price levels but also global 
macroeconomic and geopolitical 
developments, structural changes 
in market dynamics, and other fuel-
hedging strategies applied in the 
aviation industry.

When necessary, the 
hedging methodology is updated in 
line with these analyses.

The fact that revenues and expenses

The Company manages a debt 
portfolio comprising long-term 
fixed- and floating-rate borrowings to 
support investments, primarily aircraft 
acquisitions, and working capital 
needs.

At the same time, cash assets 
are managed within the portfolio 
management strategy framework to 
maintain an optimal balance between 
maturity and return.

The consolidated impact that changes 
in interest rates could have on financing 
costs and portfolio returns is regularly 
analyzed.

When deemed necessary, 
hedging transactions are implemented 
using swap and option-based 
derivative instruments to keep interest 
obligations arising from variable-rate 
financing at a controllable level.

losses that could arise if financial

maximum volume of transactions 
that can be conducted with each 
financial institution is determined in 
line with these methodologies, and 
in this way, counterparty risk within 
the financial system is managed in a 
controlled manner by diversifying risk 
concentration.

award to its members on accumulated mileage 
earned from flights. Miles are recognized as a 
separately identifiable component of each sale 
transactions. Frequent flyer program liabilities 
amounted to USD302 million in the consolidated

based on the fair value of the awarded miles. The

the awards for which they could be redeemed. The 
amount deferred is recognized as revenue when

when the Group does not expect that the miles to be 
redeemed by its customers (“breakage”).

As of 31 December 2025, an adjustment has been made in accordance with the requirements of IAS 29, 
Financial Reporting in Hyperinflationary Economies (“IAS29”) regarding the changes in the general 
purchasing power of TL. In terms of IAS 29 it is required that financial statements prepared in the currency 
in circulation in the economy with hyperinflation should be expressed in the unit of measurement valid at 
the balance sheet date, and the amounts in comparative periods should be prepared in the same way. One of 
the requirements for the application of IAS 29 is a three-year cumulative inflation rate approaching or 
exceeding 100%. The correction was made using the correction factor obtained from the Consumer Price 
Index in Türkiye published by Turkish Statistical Institute (“TUIK”). The indices and adjustment factors 
used to prepare the consolidated financial statements are as follows:

The main procedures for the above-mentioned restatement are as follows:

 
Financial statements prepared in the currency of a hyperinflationary economy are stated in terms of the 
measuring unit current at the balance sheet date, and corresponding figures for previous periods are 
restated in the same terms.

 
Monetary assets and liabilities that are carried at amounts current at the balance sheet date are not 
restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet 
date.

 
Monetary assets and liabilities that are carried at amounts current at the balance sheet date are not 
restated because they are already expressed in terms of the monetary unit current at the balance sheet 
date.

 
Non-monetary assets and liabilities that are not carried at amounts current at the balance sheet date and 
components of equity are restated by applying the relevant monthly conversion factors.

 
All items in the statement of profit or loss are restated by applying the relevant conversion factors.

 
All items in the balance sheet, statement of profit or loss and other comprehensive income of the 
subsidiaries whose functional currencies are TL are translated into USD using the closing rate as of 31 
December 2025. The combined effect of the restating in accordance with IAS 29 and translation in 
accordance with IAS 21 is presented as currency translation reserve in other comprehensive income.

2.3 Summary of Significant Accounting Policies

2.3.1 
Revenue

Group recognizes revenue when the goods or services is transferred to the customer and when performance 
obligation is fulfilled. Goods is counted to be transferred when the control belongs to the customer.

Group recognizes revenue based on the following main principles:

(a) Identification of customer contracts,

(b) Identification of performance obligations,

(c) Determination of transaction price in the contract,

(d) Allocation of price to performance obligations,

(e) Recognition of revenue when the performance obligations are fulfilled.

Group recognized revenue from its customers only when all of the following criteria are met:

(c) Determination of transaction price in the contract,

(d) Allocation of price to performance obligations,

(e) Recognition of revenue when the performance obligations are fulfilled.

Group recognized revenue from its customers only when all of the following criteria are met:

(a) The parties to the contract have approved the contract (in writing, orally or in accordance with other 
 customary business practices) and are committed to perform their respective obligations,

(b) Group can identify each party’s rights regarding the goods or services to be transferred,

(c) Group can identify the payment terms for the goods or services to be transferred;

(d) The contract has commercial substance,

(e) It is probable that Group will collect the consideration to which it will be entitled in exchange for the 
goods or services that will be transferred to the customer. In evaluating whether collectability of an amount 
of consideration is probable, an entity shall consider only the customer’s ability and intention to pay that 
amount of consideration when it is due. 
Services provided:

Revenue is measured at the fair value of the consideration received or to be received. Passenger fares and 
cargo revenues are recognized as operating revenue when the transportation service is provided. Tickets 
sold but not used (unflown) yet are recognized as passenger flight liabilities in deferred income as a 
contract liability in accordance with IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers.

The Group uses estimates based on historical statistics and data for unredeemed tickets. Total estimated 
amount of unredeemed tickets are recognized as revenue. Agency commissions relating to the passenger 
revenue are recognized as expense when the transportation service is provided.

Aircraft maintenance and infrastructure support services are recognized on accrual basis at the fair value of 
the amount collected or to be collected based on the assumptions that delivery is realized, the income can 
be reliably determined and the inflow of the economic benefits related with the transaction to the Group is 
probable.

Aircraft maintenance and infrastructure support services are recognized on accrual basis at the fair value of 
the amount collected or to be collected based on the assumptions that delivery is realized, the income can

Tickets for which the passenger is not expected to exercise their rights under the ticket contract with the

Tickets that expire unused represent unexercised passenger rights and are often referred 
to as passenger ticket breakage.

The Group recognizes breakage (or unexercised rights) as revenue.

Since 
the break date of these specific tickets can not be identified ultimately, the Group estimates and recognizes 
the expected breakage amount by using historical data and trends.

The data used for the estimation for the 
amount of unredeemed tickets is revised under the IFRS 15 and provisional ticket breakage revenue is 
calculated with the tickets not flown on their scheduled flight date.

b) Ticket Reissue Revenue 
Each fare types provided by the Group have its own conditions attached, which may include it being 
restricted, upgradeable or refundable.

A change fee may apply if passengers need to make a change to their 
booking, cancel flights or buy replacement tickets.

A change fee may apply if passengers need to make a change to their 
booking, cancel flights or buy replacement tickets.

The change service is not considered distinctly because 
the customer cannot benefit from it without taking the flight.

Although the change service is provided in 
advance of the flight, the benefit from it is not provided until the customer takes the flight.

As a result, the

Frequent Flyer Program 
The Group provides a frequent flyer program (FFP) named “Miles and Smiles” in the form of free travel

Miles earned by flights are recognized as a separately 
identifiable component of the revenue.

The amount deferred as a liability is measured based on the fair value of the awarded miles.

The fair value 
is measured on the basis of the value of the awards for which they could be redeemed.

The amount deferred 
is recognized as revenue on redemption of the points including a portion of the points that the Group does 
not expect to be redeemed by the customers (“breakage”).

The Group also sells mileage credits to participating partners in “Miles and Smiles” program.

Revenue is 
recognized when transportation is provided.

Net realizable value represents the

The real estate projects under development and construction comprise the direct and indirect costs

2.3.4 Leases

At inception of a contract, the Group assesses whether a contract is, or contains a lease. A contract is, or 
contains, a lease if the contract conveys the right to control the use of an identified asset for a period of 
time in exchange for consideration. To assess whether a contract conveys the right to control the use of an 
identified asset. The Group assess whether:

a) The contract involved the use of an identified asset – this may be specified explicitly or implicitly.

b) The asset should be physically distinct or represent substantially all of the capacity of a physically 
distinct asset, If the supplier has a substantive substitution right, the asset is not identified.

b) The asset should be physically distinct or represent substantially all of the capacity of a physically 
distinct asset, If the supplier has a substantive substitution right, the asset is not identified.

c) The Group has the right to obtain substantially all of the economic benefits from the use of an asset 
throughout the period of use; and 
d) The Group has the right to direct use of the asset, The Group concludes to have the right of use, when it 
is predetermined how and for what purpose the Group will use the asset. The Group has the right to direct 
use of asset if either:

The Group applies hedge accounting to these transactions, as they are designated to hedge against cash

liabilities are recognized in other comprehensive income and presented in cash flow hedge reserve under

2.3.10 Earnings per Share

Earnings per share are calculated by dividing net profit by weighted average number of shares outstanding 
in the relevant period. In Türkiye, companies are allowed to increase their capital by distributing free shares 
to shareholders from accumulated profits. In calculation of earnings per share, such free shares are 
considered as issued shares. Therefore, weighted average number of shares in the calculation of earnings 
per share is found by applying distribution of free shares retrospectively.

Dividends

Ordinary shares are classified as equity. Dividends on ordinary shares are recognized in equity in the period 
in which they are declared.

2.3.11 Events After the Reporting Date

Events after the balance sheet date are those events, which occur between the balance sheet date and the 
date when the consolidated financial statements are authorized for issue.

If adjustment is necessary for such events, the Group’s consolidated financial statements are adjusted to 
reflect such events.

2.3.12 Provisions, Contingent Liabilities, Contingent Assets

Provisions are recognized when the Group has a present obligation as a result of a past event, and it is 
probable that the Group will be required to settle that obligation, and a reliable estimate can be made of the 
amount of the obligation.

The amount recognized as a provision is the best estimate of the consideration required to settle the present 
obligation at the balance sheet date, taking into account the risks and uncertainties surrounding the 
obligation.

Where a provision is measured using the cash flows estimated to settle the present obligation, its carrying 
amount is the present value of those cash flows. When some or all of the economic benefits required to 
settle a provision are expected to be recovered from a third party, the receivable is recognized as an asset if 
it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received and the amount of the receivable can be measured 
reliably.

Investment properties are held to obtain rent and/or appreciation revenue and reflect the amounts remaining

2.3.15 Taxation and Deferred Tax 
Turkish tax legislation does not permit a parent company and its subsidiary to file a consolidated tax return.

2.3.15 Taxation and Deferred Tax (cont’d)

Deferred Tax

Deferred tax is recognized on differences between the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities in the 
financial statements and the corresponding tax bases which is used in the computation of taxable profit, and 
is accounted for using the balance sheet liability method.

Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognized for all taxable temporary differences and deferred tax 
assets are recognized for all deductible temporary differences to the extent that it is probable that taxable 
profits will be available against which those deductible temporary differences can be utilized. Such assets 
and liabilities are not recognized if the temporary difference arises from goodwill or from the initial 
recognition (other than in a business combination) of other assets and liabilities in a transaction that affects 
neither the taxable profit nor the accounting profit.

Deferred tax liabilities are generally recognized for all taxable temporary differences and deferred tax 
assets are recognized for all deductible temporary differences to the extent that it is probable that taxable 
profits will be available against which those deductible temporary differences can be utilized. Such assets 
and liabilities are not recognized if the temporary difference arises from goodwill or from the initial 
recognition (other than in a business combination) of other assets and liabilities in a transaction that affects 
neither the taxable profit nor the accounting profit.

Deferred tax liabilities are recognized for taxable temporary differences associated with investments in 
subsidiaries and affiliates, and interests in joint ventures, except where the Group is able to control the 
reversal of the temporary difference and it is probable that the temporary difference will not reverse in the 
foreseeable future. Deferred tax assets arising from deductible temporary differences associated with such 
investments and interests are only recognized to the extent that it is probable that there will be sufficient 
taxable profits against which to utilize the benefits of the temporary differences and they are expected to 
reverse in the foreseeable future.

The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each balance sheet date and reduced to the extent 
that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profits will be available to allow all or part of the asset to 
be recovered.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period in 
which the liability is settled or the asset realized, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted 
or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date. The measurement of deferred tax liabilities and assets 
reflects the tax consequences that would follow from the manner in which the Group expects, at the 
reporting date, to recover or settle the carrying amount of its assets and liabilities.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply in the period in 
which the liability is settled or the asset realized, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted 
or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date. The measurement of deferred tax liabilities and assets 
reflects the tax consequences that would follow from the manner in which the Group expects, at the 
reporting date, to recover or settle the carrying amount of its assets and liabilities.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are offset when there is a legally enforceable right to set off current tax 
assets against current tax liabilities and when they relate to income taxes levied by the same taxation 
authority and the Group intends to settle its current tax assets and liabilities on a net basis. 
Current and deferred tax for the year 
Current and deferred tax is recognized as income or expense in the consolidated statement of profit or loss, 
except to the extent that it relates to items recognized directly in equity or other comprehensive income, or 
where they arise from the initial accounting for a business combination. In the case of a business 
combination, the tax effect is taken into account in calculating goodwill or determining the excess of the 
acquirer’s interest in the net fair value of the acquirer’s identifiable assets, liabilities and contingent 
liabilities over cost.

2.3.16 Government Grants 
Government grants are not recognized until there is reasonable assurance that the Group will comply with 
the conditions attaching to them and that the grants will be received. Government grants are recognized in 
profit or loss on a systematic basis over the periods in which the Group recognizes as expenses the related 
costs for which the grants are intended to compensate.

2.3 Summary of Significant Accounting Policies (cont’d)

2.3.16 Government Grants (cont’d)

Specifically, government grants whose primary condition is that the Group should purchase, construct or 
otherwise acquire non-current assets are recognized profit or loss on a systematic and rational basis over 
the useful lives of the related assets.

Government grants that are receivable as compensation for expenses or losses already incurred or for the 
purpose of giving immediate financial support to the Group with no future related costs are recognized in 
profit or loss in the period in which they become receivable.

2.3.17 Employee Benefits / Retirement Pay Provision

2.3.17 Employee Benefits / Retirement Pay Provision

Under Turkish law and union agreements, lump sum payments are made to employees retiring or 
involuntarily leaving the Group. Such payments are considered as being part of defined retirement benefit 
plan as per International Accounting Standard 19 (revised) “Employee Benefits” (“IAS 19”).

The retirement benefit obligation recognized in the balance sheet represents the present value of the defined 
benefit obligation as adjusted for unrecognized actuarial gains and losses. Actuarial gains and losses are 
accounted as other comprehensive income.

2.3.18 Maintenance and Repair Cost

Regular maintenance and repair costs for owned and leased assets are charged to cost of sales as incurred. 
Aircraft and engine overhaul maintenance checks for owned and leased aircrafts are capitalized and 
depreciated over the shorter of the remaining period to the following overhaul maintenance checks or the 
remaining useful life of the aircraft. For aircraft held under operating leases the Group is contractually 
committed to either return the aircraft in a certain condition or to compensate the lessor upon return of the 
aircraft. The estimated airframes and engine maintenance costs are accrued and charges to profit or loss 
over the lease term, based on the present value of the estimated future cost of the major airframe overhaul, 
engine maintenance calculated by reference to hours or order operated during the year.

Payments made to lessors under lease agreements in respect of engine maintenance reserves and major 
overhaul contributions are recognized as prepaid engine maintenance expenses.

2.3.19 Statement of Cash Flows

In statement of cash flows, cash flows are classified according to operating, investing and financing 
activities.

In the Statement of Cash Flow, exchange rate differences arising in the "Cash and Cash Equivalents" 
section are reclassified from the "Adjustments for Unrealised Foreign Exchange Gains" section to the " 
Effects of Foreign Exchange on Cash and Cash Equivalents" section.

In the Statement of Cash Flow, exchange rate differences arising in the "Cash and Cash Equivalents"

Transactions between the Group and TFS Akaryakıt and THY Opet are related to the supply of aircraft 
fuel; transactions between the Group and Turkish DO&CO are related to catering services; transactions 
between the Group and SunExpress are related to aircraft transportation, seat sales operations and 
maintenance services; transactions between the Group and TGS are related to ground, support and 
technology services; transactions between the Group and TEC are related to engine maintenance services; 
transactions between the Group and PTT are related to cargo transportation; transactions between the 
Group and Halkbank, Ziraat Bankası, Vakıf Bank and Ziraat Katılım are related to banking services; 
transactions between the Group and Air Albania are related to aircraft transportation; transactions between 
the Group and Turkcell and, Türk Telekom are related to telecommunication services; transactions between 
the Group and Goodrich are related to maintenance services; transactions between the Group and Türkiye 
Sigorta are related to insurance services; transactions between the Group and We World Express are related 
to cargo transportation and transactions between the Group. Receivables from related parties are not 
collateralized and maturity of trade receivables is 30 days.

The total amount of all short-term benefits, including salaries, bonuses, vehicles allocated for their use and 
communication expenses provided for the Board Members, General Managers and Deputy General 
Managers of the Group is USD 18 for the period between 1 January - 31 December 2025 (1 January- 31 
December 2024: USD 19).

Retirement pay liability is not subject to any funding legally. Provisions for retirement pay liability are 
calculated by estimating the present value of probable liability that will arise due to the retirement of 
employees.

IAS 19 (“Employee Benefits”) stipulates the progress of the Group’s liabilities by use of actuarial valuation 
methods under defined benefit plans. Actuarial assumptions used in calculation of total liabilities are described 
as follows:

The critical assumption is that the maximum liability amount increases in accordance with the inflation rate for 
every service year. Provisions in the accompanying consolidated financial statements as of 31 December 2025 
are calculated by estimating the present value of liabilities due to the retirement of employees. Provisions in the 
relevant balance sheet dates are calculated with the assumptions of 24.61% annual inflation rate (31 December 
2024: 24.95%) and 29.82% interest rate (31 December 2024: 29.32%). Estimated amount of non-paid 
retirement pay retained in the Group due to voluntary leaves is assumed as 2.33% (31 December 2024: 2.20%). 
Ceiling for retirement pay is revised semi-annually. Ceiling amount of USD 1,513 (full) (equivalent to TL 
64,949 (full)) which has been in effect since 1 January 2026, is used in the calculation of the Group’s provision

SHAREHOLDERS’ EQUITY (cont’d)

Restricted Profit Reserves 
Turkish Commercial Code (TCC) stipulates that the general legal reserve is appropriated out of statutory 
profits at the rate of 5% per annum, until the total reserve reaches 20% of the Group’s paid-in share capital. 
Additionally, not limited with 20% of paid-in share capital, the general legal reserve is appropriated at the 
rate of 10% per annum of all cash dividends in excess of 5% of the paid-in share capital. Under TCC, the 
legal reserves can only be used to offset losses, to sustain business when conditions worsen, to prevent 
unemployment and are not available for any other usage unless they exceed 50% of paid-in share capital.

In accordance with Article 520 of the Turkish Commercial Code, the Group is required to allocate a reserve 
fund in an amount that covers the purchase value for its own shares purchased.

Gains/Losses from Cash Flow Hedges

Hedge gain/losses against cash flow risk arise from the accounting of the changes in the fair values of 
effective derivative financial instruments designated against financial risks of future cash flows under 
equity. Total of deferred gain/loss arising from hedging against financial risk is accounted in profit or loss 
when the hedged item impacts profit or loss.

Euro for investment financing are designated as cash flow hedge against exchange rate risk due to highly 
probable future same foreign currency revenues. Group’s revenue denominated in Euro, Chinese Yuan and 
Swiss Franc fully covered borrowings of such foreign currency, while Japanese Yen revenue covered %40 
of borrowings. In this context, exchange differences arising from such these loans repayment are taken to

exemptions.

32. EARNINGS PER SHARE

Earnings per share disclosed in the consolidated profit or loss and other comprehensive income is

outstanding during the relevant period.

In Türkiye, companies can increase their share capital by making a pro-rata distribution of shares (“bonus 
interest”) to existing shareholders from retained earnings. For the purpose of earnings per share 
computations, such bonus shares are regarded as issued shares. Accordingly, the weighted average number 
of shares outstanding during the years has been adjusted in respect of bonus shares issued without a 
corresponding change in resources, by giving them retroactive effect for the year in which they were issued 
and for each earlier year.

(a) Capital risk management

The Group manages its capital to ensure that entities in the Group will be able to continue as a going 
concern while maximizing the return to stakeholders through the optimization of the debt and equity 
balance.

The capital structure of the Group consists of debt, which includes the borrowings disclosed in Note 7, cash 
and cash equivalents and equity attributable to equity holders of the parent, comprising issued capital, 
reserves and retained earnings.

The Board of Directors of the Group periodically reviews the capital structure. During these analyses, the 
Board assesses the risks associated with each class of capital along with cost of capital. Based on the 
review of the Board of Directors, the Group aims to balance its overall capital structure through the issue of 
new debt or the redemption of existing debt. The overall strategy of the Group has not changed compared 
to 2024.

The Group’s credit risk is related to its receivables, cash and derivative financial assets. The balance shown in the consolidated balance sheet is the result of 
the net amount after deducting the doubtful receivables arisen from the Group management’s forecasts based on previous experience and current economy 
conditions. Since the customers are diversified, the Group’s credit risk is dispersed and there is no material credit risk concentration.

The main responsibility for liquidity risk management rests with the Board of Directors. The Board 
designed an appropriate risk management policy for short, medium and long term funding and liquidity 
necessities of the Group management. The Group manages liquidity risk by maintaining adequate reserves, 
banking facilities and reserve borrowing facilities by continuously monitoring forecast and actual cash 
flows and matching the maturity profiles of financial assets and liabilities.

Interest rate sensitivity

The following sensitivity analysis are done considering the interest rate exposure in the reporting date and 
possible changes on this rate and are fixed during all reporting period. Group management checks out 
possible effects that may arise when Sofr and Euribor rates, which are the basis for floating interest rates, 
fluctuate 0.5% and reports the effects to the top management.

Assuming that there is a 0.5% increase in Sofr and Euribor interest rates and all other floatings are kept 
constant:

Current profit before tax of the Group for the year will decrease by USD 33 (For the year ended 31 
December 2024 profit before tax will decrease by USD 27). In contrast, if Sofr and Euribor interest rate 
decrease by 0.5%, profit before tax will increase by the same amounts.

Current profit before tax of the Group for the year will decrease by USD 33 (For the year ended 31 
December 2024 profit before tax will decrease by USD 27). In contrast, if Sofr and Euribor interest rate 
decrease by 0.5%, profit before tax will increase by the same amounts.

Moreover, as a result of the interest rate swap contracts against cash flow risks, in the event of a 0.5% 
increase in the Sofr and Euribor interest rates, the shareholders’ equity of the Group will be affected less 
then USD 1, excluding the deferred tax effect. (For the year ended 31 December 2024 the shareholders’ 
equity of the Group will increase by USD 1, excluding the deferred tax effect.) In the event of a 0.5% 
decrease in the Sofr and Euribor interest rates, the shareholders’ equity of the Group will decrease by the 
same amounts, excluding the deferred tax effect. 
b.4.3) Fuel prices sensitivity 
As explained in Note 35, Group has entered into forward fuel purchase contracts in order to hedge cash 
flow risks arising from fuel purchases. Due to forward fuel purchase contracts subject to hedge accounting, 
as a result of a 10% increase in fuel prices, the shareholders’ equity of the Group will increase by USD 47, 
excluding the deferred tax effect. (For the year ended 31 December 2024, the shareholders’ equity of the 
Group will increase by USD 52 excluding deferred tax effect.)

In case of a 10% decrease in fuel prices, the shareholders’ equity of the Group will decrease by USD 51, 
excluding the deferred tax effect. (For the year ended 31 December 2024, the shareholders’ equity of the 
Group will decrease by USD 54, excluding deferred tax effect.)

Derivative Instruments and Hedging Transactions 
The financial risk management strategy of the Group aims to ensure a healthy cash flow and liquidity in the 
future.

For this purpose, derivative financial instruments such as currency forwards, currency options, 
interest rate swaps, interest rate options, oil options and oil swaps are used to protect against the financial 
risks arising from the fluctuation of exchange rates, interest rates and jet fuel price.

The floating-rate financial liabilities of the Group are explained in Note 34 b.4.2.

In order to keep interest 
costs at an affordable level, the Group has hedged approximately 4% of floating rate USD, JPY, CNY, 
CHF and Euro denominated liabilities arising from financial leasing activities.

Effective part of the change 
in the fair values of those derivative instruments for cash flows risks of floating-rate finance lease liabilities 
are recognized in other comprehensive income and presented in cash flow hedge reserve under the 
shareholders’ equity, in accordance with hedge accounting.

Within the scope of the financial risk management strategy, the Group started fuel price risk hedging in 
2009, in order to manage the cash flow effect that may arise from the fluctuation of the fuel price.

Fuel 
price risk management strategy was updated several times over the years with the experience gained.

Fuel 
price risk management strategy was updated several times over the years with the experience gained.

In 
accordance with the Group’s latest BOD resolution issued on 14 July 2017, hedging transactions are 
executed for the tenor of at most 24 months and up to 60% of the forecasted fuel consumption of the 
following month.

Also with this resolution, premium paid options have been included to the instrument list 
for the first time, in addition to formerly used swap and zero-cost option structures.

The tenor, ratio and 
instrument to-be-used are chosen based on the current market conditions and future expectations.

As a 
result of these changes, hedging strategy has become more flexible and accommodative to fuel market 
conditions.

It is aimed to either fix the fuel price or keep it in a restrained range.

The effective portion of 
fair value of fuel hedge contracts for cash flow hedge is recognized in other comprehensive income and 
presented in cash flow hedge reserve under the shareholders’ equity, in accordance with hedge accounting.

Derivative Instruments and Hedging Transactions (cont’d)

The mismatch between Group’s income and expense currencies causes to the exchange rate risk. In order to 
manage this risk resulted from the fluctuations of the FX market, the Group started to implement exchange 
rate risk hedging in 2013. Exchange rate risk management strategy of the Group was updated in 2015 and 
2018 as a result of the gained experience and the needs. In order to manage this risk resulted from the 
fluctuations of the FX market, the Group started to implement exchange rate risk hedging. Since the Group 
is short in JPY, strategy mainly aims to decrease the amount of short position in JPY with the long position 
in USD via the derivative instruments. Only forwards are used for USD/JPY transactions. Other derivative 
instruments can be used in accordance with the market conditions, especially zero-cost option structures. In 
accordance with the strategy, current market conditions and future expectations are analyzed dynamically, 
and the hedge tenor, ratio and instrument to be used are determined accordingly. With these transactions, 
the Company aims to fix the exchange rate at a single level or to keep it within a certain range. The 
effective portion of fair value of currency hedge contracts for cash flow hedge is recognized in other 
comprehensive income and presented in cash flow hedge reserve under the shareholders’ equity, in 
accordance with hedge accounting.

As of 2025, financial lease liabilities in Japanese Yen, Swiss Franc, Chinese Yuan and Euro for investment 
financing are designated as cash flow hedge against exchange rate risk due to highly probable future same 
foreign currency revenues. Group’s revenue denominated in Chinese Yuan, Euro and Swiss Franc fully 
covered borrowings of such foreign currency while Japanese Yen revenue covered 40% of borrowings. In 
this context, exchange differences arising from such these loans repayment are taken to equity and 
recognized in other comprehensive income.

SAF Supply
The global supply of Sustainable 
Aviation Fuel (SAF), which is a critical 
tool in decarbonizing the aviation 
sector, remains limited.

According to 
International Air Transport Association 
(IATA) data, SAF production reached 
approximately 1.9 million tons (Mt) in 
2025, nearly doubling compared to 
2024.

This amount corresponds to only 
0.6% of total jet fuel consumption.

This amount corresponds to only 
0.6% of total jet fuel consumption.

For 2026, production is projected to 
reach 2.4 million tons and to account 
for approximately 0.8% of total jet 
fuel consumption.

Limited supply 
conditions make access to SAF more 
difficult and increase costs.

With 
SAF prices being 2 to 4 times higher 
than conventional jet fuel prices, the 
importance of financial planning and 
procurement strategies increases for 
airlines.

In this context, long-term 
planning, supply chain collaboration 
and alternative procurement models 
come to the fore to effectively manage 
uncertainties in SAF supply.

Taking these challenges into account, 
the Company voluntarily used SAF for 
the first time on 2 February 2022 on 
the Istanbul-Paris route.

Since then, it 
has aimed to increase SAF use, which 
has been maintained both voluntarily 
and within the scope of mandatory 
SAF regulations, depending on SAF 
availability.

To secure access to SAF, 
different models including long-term 
supply agreements, investment and 
offtake options are being evaluated.

In this direction, analysis and planning 
activities are carried out to establish 
a sustainable SAF supply portfolio.

In 
line with the Group’s growth plans, the 
SAF strategy covering short, medium 
and long-term targets was completed 
in 2025.

To develop SAF production capacity 
in Türkiye and support different 
production technologies, it is planned 
to evaluate long-term procurement 
models with domestic producers.

This 
approach aims both to incentivize 
domestic SAF production and to 
strengthen the local supply chain.

These publicly disclosed collaborations 
support the targets of structuring 
domestically sourced SAF supply and 
strengthening supply continuity.

initiatives are expected to provide a 
basis for increasing SAF supply and 
assessing opportunities for operational 
use.

Effects on Financial Position, 
Financial Performance, and Cash 
Flows
Volatility experienced in the aviation 
sector in previous years indicates that 
similar situations may occur in the 
coming years.

Therefore, the likelihood 
of deviations in long-term projections 
is also high.

This would cause long-
term projections to differ significantly 
from actual results and could lead 
readers of financial and sustainability 
reports to make misleading 
assessments.

For this reason, when 
analyzing the financial statement 
impacts of sustainability-related risks, 
the Group has excluded long-term 
effects from the scope of the analysis.

The Group evaluates its financial 
position based on total assets and its 
financial performance based on net 
profit for the period, and regularly 
analyzes the current and potential 
impacts of sustainability-related risks 
and opportunities on these indicators, 
reflecting them in its financial 
statements in accordance with the 
relevant accounting standards.

The Group prepares its statement of 
cash flows using the indirect method 
in accordance with TAS 7 Statement of 
Cash Flows.

Under this method, cash 
flows are derived from profit for the 
period.

Accordingly, all transactions 
affecting “Profit for the Period 
from Continuing Operations” in the 
statement of profit or loss will affect 
the statement of cash flows (under the 
“Net Cash from Operating Activities” 
sub heading) in the same proportion.

Within this analysis process, the 
financial impacts of risks and 
opportunities are directly taken into 
account.

When determining the 
impact level of risks, their effects on 
the Group’s financial position, financial 
performance and cash flows are 
considered as the basis.

When determining the 
impact level of risks, their effects on

performance and cash flows are 
considered as the basis.

In determining impact levels, an 
assessment is made based on the 
magnitude of the financial impacts. 
Risks that could cause a change of 
5% or more in the Group’s relevant 
financial indicators are assessed as 
very high impact, risks that could 
cause a change of above 4% are 
assessed as high impact, impacts at 
the 3% level are assessed as medium 
impact, and impacts at 2% and below 
are assessed as low impact. During 
the reporting period, the materiality 
threshold and methodology were 
reassessed and it was determined 
that no changes were required for the 
relevant period.

Risks and opportunities identified as a 
result of the assessment are submitted 
to senior management and, taking 
their financial impacts into account, 
are incorporated into decision-making 
processes. Accordingly, climate-related 
risks and opportunities are directly 
integrated into the Group’s financial 
planning.

Scenario Analyses
Within the scope of scenario analyses, the scenario set used in identifying and prioritizing climate-related risks and 
opportunities was designed to represent a Paris Agreement-aligned <2°C scenario and a >4°C scenario in which the 
temperature increase cannot be limited. Accordingly, assumptions, quantitative metrics and supporting sources for key 
drivers such as carbon regulations and energy policies, aviation sector-specific policies and mechanisms, macroeconomic 
trends, national or regional variables, energy use and technological developments are presented in the tables below. Outputs 
obtained from the scenario analyses are used as reference points in assessing the impacts of THY’s climate-related risks and 
opportunities in the short, medium and long-term, reflecting these impacts in the resilience assessment, and designing the 
action set in response to risks and opportunities. The assessment results are linked in an integrated flow within the relevant 
disclosures of the report.

Carbon 
Credits
Carbon offsetting is positioned as a policy tool that 
complements in-sector emissions reduction measures 
in the aviation sector’s net zero pathway.

ICAO’s CORSIA 
framework, in addition to MRV of emissions from 
international flights, defines carbon credits that may 
be used for compliance through the “CORSIA Eligible 
Emissions Units” list approved by the ICAO Council and 
is based on an eligibility criteria approach to ensure the 
environmental integrity of these units.

CORSIA also provides a verification framework that 
contributes to reducing carbon credit needs by defining a 
minimum 10% net greenhouse gas reduction threshold on 
a life-cycle basis for SAF and lower carbon aviation fuels 
through the “CORSIA Sustainability Criteria for CORSIA 
Eligible Fuels” document dated 27 June 2025.

This integrated framework treats carbon credits, in a Paris-
aligned transition (<2°C), as a measurable and auditable 
incentive and compliance mechanism for residual 
emissions.

RISK NO: TR1
Emerging Sustainable Aviation 
Fuel (SAF) mandates across 
different regions and countries
Description:
The increasing number of regulations 
mandating the use of SAF across 
different regions and countries 
constitutes one of the climate 
transition risks that could reasonably 
be expected to affect the Group’s 
future financial capacity in the 
short, medium, and long-term. The 
expansion of the regulatory framework 
gradually increases SAF blending 
requirements, making SAF supply 
conditions and cost management key 
considerations in strategic planning. 
The risk assessment is conducted 
under the assumptions of a Paris 
Agreement-aligned world (<2°C) and 
a world where temperature increase 
cannot be limited (>4°C), as defined in 
the Scenario Analysis section, taking 
into account regulatory developments 
and the associated cost impact 
channels.

Time Horizon: Short/Medium/Long
Effects on Business Model and 
Value Chain
Within the scope of ReFuelEU 
Aviation, a minimum 2% SAF blending 
requirement for flights departing 
from European Union (EU) airports 
entered into force in 2025, and the 
required share is planned to increase 
gradually to 70% by 2050.

Through this 
obligation imposed on fuel suppliers, 
in addition to SAF, synthetic fuel 
(e-fuel, PtL) sub-targets have also 
been introduced, to be implemented 
starting from 2030.

In the United Kingdom, under the 
SAF Mandate, the requirement begins 
at 2% in 2025 and is structured to 
increase to 10.6% by 2030 and 23.7% by 
2040.

In Türkiye, the Directorate General of 
Civil Aviation (DGCA) introduced a SAF 
usage requirement for international 
flights departing from Türkiye through 
the SHT-SAF directive published in 
2025.

In Türkiye, the Directorate General of 
Civil Aviation (DGCA) introduced a SAF 
usage requirement for international 
flights departing from Türkiye through 
the SHT-SAF directive published in 
2025.

With this instruction, it is aimed to 
use SAF in an amount that will meet the 
minimum emission reduction values to 
be announced annually by the Turkish 
DGCA as of 2026.

In Asia, under Singapore’s SAF Levy 
regulation, the use of SAF on flights will 
become mandatory as of 2026, starting 
a 1% target, and is expected to increase 
towards a 3% to 5% range by 2030.

In 
South Korea, a mandatory framework 
has been announced that starts with 
a 1% blending ratio for international 
departing flights as of 2027, increasing 
to 3%- 5% by 2030 and to 7%- 10% by 
2035.

These regulatory developments 
indicate a growing demand for SAF 
and an increasing need for scaling 
up the supply chain.

Considering the 
geographical distribution of SAF supply 
together with limited production 
capacity, feedstock constraints, 
logistics and refueling infrastructure, 
and certification and compliance 
requirements, the impacts are expected 
to concentrate across the value chain, 
particularly in fuel procurement, 
contract management, cost planning, 
and operational planning processes.

In this context, the increasing SAF 
mandates across different regions 
have the potential to create upward 
pressure on operational costs.

However, 
the magnitude of the cost impact will 
depend on SAF supply availability, 
procurement conditions, price 
dynamics, and the implementation 
timelines of regulatory obligations.

(TSRS 2, 15b, 13a&b)

Under 
CORSIA, offsetting obligations are 
calculated based on sectoral growth 
relative to 2019 and are determined 
by applying the annual Sector’s 
Growth Factor (SGF) published by 
ICAO to the relevant year’s emissions.

Authorization (LoA) processes issued 
by host countries.

These processes 
aim to prevent double counting under 
Article 6 of the Paris Agreement;

however, administrative uncertainties 
in implementation may increase the 
risks of supply constraints and price 
volatility.

Within the scope of this risk, unit prices 
of allowances used under emissions 
trading systems (ETS), market supply 
demand balance, free allocation 
volumes and regulatory revisions may 
also affect the level of compliance 
costs.

The scenario analysis conducted by 
the Group to assess its climate-related 
risks and opportunities provides the 
ability to evaluate the organization’s 
resilience to climate change.

The 
boundaries of the analysis undertaken 
to identify climate resilience span 
the range between two endpoints: 
scenarios aligned with the Paris 
Agreement that present a world 
where global temperature increase is 
limited to 1.5°C, namely IEA NZE 2050 
and IPCC SSP1-2.6, and scenarios that 
present a world where temperature 
increase cannot be limited to 2°C and 
an increase above 3 to 4°C is observed, 
namely IEA STEPS and IPCC SSP5-
8.5.

The optimistic scenarios aligned 
with the Paris Agreement assume a 
shift towards a carbon neutral future, 
a transition to renewable energy, 
and a rapid phase out of fossil fuels.

The steps and actions required for 
these projections to materialize form 
the basis of the Group’s long-term 
strategies.

However, the feasibility of 
this approach depends on the scope 
and effectiveness of carbon pricing 
mechanisms and on establishing 
regulatory frameworks that support 
companies’ transition from fossil 
fuels to low carbon energy sources.

At the same time, uncertainty in 
compliance with climate policies 
and environmental regulations can 
challenge resilience by affecting 
future profitability and cost structure.

For this reason, pessimistic scenario 
projections with higher temperature 
increases are also considered within 
the analysis, and measures and actions 
the Group can take against these 
developments are taken into account 
in strategic planning.

For example, 
weak climate-related regulations may 
result in carbon intensive activities 
continuing as usual, leading to 
accelerated emissions growth.

Severe 
atmospheric conditions that create 
critical physical risks may, over time, 
act as a trigger for increased carbon 
pricing and regulation.

This may cause 
the business to face significant costs 
and financial uncertainty.

To mitigate such risks, it is important 
for the Group to consider all 
possibilities in its assessments.

Including different climate scenarios 
in the risk assessment process 
strengthens the Group’s business 
strategies against future uncertainties.

The source of carbon credits used 
under CORSIA depends on eligibility 
criteria determined by ICAO’s 
relevant technical team.

CORSIA 
defines certification requirements 
regarding the types of projects from 
which credits may be generated.

These projects may arise from both 
nature based and technological 
solutions.

Nature based projects 
generally include forest conservation, 
afforestation, reforestation, and other 
ecosystem restoration initiatives, while 
technological carbon removal includes 
methods such as carbon capture and 
storage (CCS).

CORSIA eligible emissions credits 
can be generated through carbon 
reduction or removal provided that 
they comply with principles such as 
Additionality, a realistic and credible 
baseline scenario, Permanence, and 
avoiding harm in a clear manner.

To ensure the reliability and integrity 
of carbon credits, the Company uses 
internationally recognized certification 
systems as a basis.

may lead to higher fuel consumption 
in flight operations.

deviations in precipitation changes 
across geographically different 
destinations.

future financial effect are as follows:
· Multiple market forecasts: The 
Company’s relevant units assessed 
Brent crude oil price projections 
through 2046 based on financial 
institutions’ and market forecasts.

· Multi-scenario analysis 1: SSP1-

pessimistic scenarios were used 
for the short and medium-term to 
provide realistic approaches.

· Sensitivity analysis: Point-based 
assessments were performed for 
Company destinations selected 
using the IPCC Interactive Atlas 
under optimistic and pessimistic 
scenarios.

· Diversification of data sources: 
An analysis was carried out by 
selecting different domestic and 
international destinations with the 
highest number of diversions and 
cancellations in collaboration with 
the meteorological research unit.

· Multi-scenario analysis 2: The 
effect of maximum temperature 
increases on payload loss was

(pessimistic) climate scenarios.

· Multi-scenario analysis 2: The 
effect of maximum temperature 
increases on payload loss was 
compared based on short and

· Data improvement and disclosure 
of limitations: A sample of long-haul 
flights departing during the hottest 
hours of the day in the summer 
schedule was analyzed using the

system.

Within this sample, payload 
losses in tons for the longest routes 
departing at the hottest hour of the 
day, where payload loss may occur 
under the 2025 summer schedule, 
were considered.
